paras: The attempted lynching of Bob Yenders took place in Rowan County, Kentucky, in late January 1888, when a number of farmers hanged Yenders from the beam above his cabin door on suspicion that he had raped a nine-year-old girl. He was cut down when word arrived that another man, John Hooper, was guilty, and one version says he survived. Papers across the country carried the story under headlines about the wrong man being hanged.

According to a letter from Rowan County, the nine-year-old daughter of Samuel Carter, described as a well-to-do farmer, was "outraged" on the morning of January 21 by "an unknown negro." The letter was received by John Martin, identified as a party to the county's Martin-Tolliver feud, and it also reported three men shot during a row at a party near Morehead on January 24.

Suspicion fell on Bob Yenders, "of the neighborhood," and a number of farmers went to his cabin and hanged him from the beam above his door. As Yenders was "in the throes of death," word reached them that John Hooper, not Yenders, was guilty, and he was cut down. A variant of the Louisville text printed in Freehold, New Jersey, said a "crowd of farmers" hanged him on the 21st and that he was cut down "in time to save his life."

The same variant said the lynchers were then looking for Hooper. No report of an arrest, inquest, or prosecution of either the farmers or Hooper appears in the coverage, and no officers are mentioned in any version.

The story reached the press as a Louisville dispatch dated January 29 to 31 and ran nearly word for word in papers from New York to Sacramento between January 30 and early February. Headlines stressed the mistake rather than the hanging: the Evening World used "They Hanged the Wrong Man," the Sacramento Daily Record-Union "An Innocent Man Lynched," and the Monmouth Inquirer "A Hairbreadth Escape Indeed." The New York Sun placed it under "A Cheerful News Budget," with the deck "Hanged the Wrong Negro."

Many papers framed the item as part of Rowan County's lawlessness, under heads such as "More Bloodshed in Rowan," "The Rowan County Trouble Renewed," and "Bloody Kentucky." Two papers, including the Big Sandy News of Louisa, Kentucky, used the deck "Three White Men Shot at a Dance, and the Wrong Colored Man Lynched for Assaulting a Little Girl," the only wording that gives the hanged man's race. None of the printed versions commented on the hanging itself, and the item later shrank to a single sentence in news summaries such as the Londonderry Sifter's.

Spellings of the victim's name varied as the wire was reset, with "Genders" in the Kentucky and Ohio papers and "Tenders" in the Indianapolis Journal. A Chicago relay in the Los Angeles Daily Herald placed the events in "Rowen county, Virginia," while the Kentucky papers and the Louisville dateline place them in Rowan County, Kentucky.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Bob Yenders
bases: A number of farmers hanged Yenders from a beam at his cabin as the suspected assailant of a child and cut him down only when told another man was guilty (A1, A12, A13).

Yenders was hanged by 'a number of farmers' acting on a suspicion of rape, with no lawful authority mentioned, but he was cut down alive and one version says his life was saved (A1, A12); no death means this was an attempted lynching, and the group's size is not given.
Every version traces to one letter from Rowan County, received by John Martin and sent out from Louisville (A2, A9, A13); the papers agree, but none is an independent report.

accounts.label: Louisville wire (letter to John Martin)
accounts.gist: A letter from Rowan County reported the Carter girl's assault by 'an unknown negro', the hanging of the suspected Yenders by farmers, and his cutting down when Hooper was named; it ran with an account of three men shot at a dance near Morehead.

accounts.label: Variant Louisville text
accounts.gist: A shorter version dated Jan. 31 said Yenders was hanged by 'a crowd of farmers' on the 21st, was cut down in time to save his life, and that the lynchers were looking for Hooper.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Louisville text nearly verbatim under headlines stressing the mistake, 'They Hanged the Wrong Man' (Evening World) and 'An Innocent Man Lynched' (Sacramento), without editorial comment on the hanging itself.
The Sun filed it under 'A Cheerful News Budget' with 'Hanged the Wrong Negro', and the Monmouth Inquirer headed it 'A Hairbreadth Escape Indeed', treating it as an ironic or narrow-escape item.
Several papers folded it into Rowan County lawlessness: 'Rowan County Crimes', 'More Bloodshed in Rowan', 'The Rowan County Trouble Renewed', 'Bloody Kentucky'.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of one name in reprints of the same letter; no paper prefers one on evidence.
